title: How resilient is Britain’s food supply?
label: 12 October 2026 · Resilience of the UK’s food supply
summary: Witnesses from farming, retail and food manufacturing and two food-policy professors told the Committee that the UK food system has so far coped with recent shocks but faces rising risks. Key problems are climate-driven harvest failures, high energy and input costs, falling investment and fragmented Government action. They called for clearer long-term strategy, better mapping of critical food infrastructure, targeted support to encourage domestic production and stronger local planning and public preparedness.

chapters.title: Big picture: resilient so far, but risks rising
chapters.takeaway: The food system has coped with recent shocks, but climate, energy costs, reduced domestic production and policy uncertainty are increasing risk.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: We’re dedicating time this week to look at the UK’s food supply resilience. I’ll start by asking: what are the biggest challenges farmers currently face?

turns.speaker: Jim Bligh
turns.text: Retailers rely on a resilient supply chain. Recent shocks—from covid to Ukraine and Iran—show the system can adapt, but risks are growing: climate, energy and water, cyber-security, rules and geopolitics.

turns.speaker: Balwinder Dhoot
turns.text: The sector has been resilient, but domestic production is slowly eroding. Trade and factory relocation mean we could rely on imports more—manageable now, but risky if the trend continues.

turns.speaker: Harry Metcalfe
turns.text: Farming varies across the country. In my arable area we’ve had four poor harvests since 2020 and 2026 was the smallest since records began. Climate variability is the immediate problem for growers.

chapters.title: Farmers’ pain: climate, cash-flow and incentives
chapters.takeaway: Arable farmers face repeated poor harvests, high input costs and removed payments, which together shrink cash flow and discourage planting.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Harry, what practical problem would make you stop growing food?

turns.speaker: Harry Metcalfe
turns.text: Cash flow. I’d already spent 74% of 2027 costs. After successive bad years, I can’t invest. Taking away basic area payments exposed farmers to world prices and big weather risk.

turns.speaker: Rupert Lowe
turns.text: Taxes, net-zero costs and other levies make farming less competitive. You’re drilling crops at a loss hoping prices or weather improve—so should Government step back or act differently?

turns.speaker: Jim Bligh
turns.text: Long-term finance and partnerships help: retailers and suppliers can offer stability for big investments. But Government policy churn weakens that certainty.

turns.speaker: Balwinder Dhoot
turns.text: Resilience needs investment. If businesses can’t make returns here, processing and production shift overseas and domestic capacity is lost.

chapters.title: Retail and processing: profit, energy and capacity
chapters.takeaway: Retailers say they prioritise British supply but face 20% higher effective tax rates and big energy cost rises that reduce investment in UK processing.

turns.speaker: Jim Bligh
turns.text: Retailers do prioritise UK sourcing and long-term partnerships with farmers. But tax and energy increases—about £8bn extra since 2024—limit investment and resilience.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Is loss of UK processing—slaughterhouses, packhouses, roasting and canning—a threat?

turns.speaker: Jim Bligh
turns.text: Yes. Some processing remains here but key inputs (like CO2 or energy-intensive processing) are vulnerable. Where processing is cheaper abroad, the supply chain shifts overseas.

turns.speaker: Balwinder Dhoot
turns.text: If processing leaves, factories won’t buy British ingredients. Energy competitiveness is central—if UK power costs are higher, investment goes elsewhere.

chapters.title: Critical infrastructure and local resilience
chapters.takeaway: Witnesses urged mapping and protecting vital food assets, better local planning and more household preparedness to avoid panic-driven shortages.

turns.speaker: Mr Betts
turns.text: Should food supply chains be on the critical national infrastructure database?

turns.speaker: Jim Bligh
turns.text: Yes. Ports, large depots, food manufacturing hubs and cold chains are strategic assets and need clear identification and protection with the Cabinet Office and DEFRA working together.

turns.speaker: Balwinder Dhoot
turns.text: You don’t need to capture every business. Identify key nodes—abattoirs, major processors, feed mills, fertiliser and CO2 supply—and test how resilient they are to fuel or grid problems.

turns.speaker: Jim Bligh
turns.text: Local resilience forums vary in capability. The best international examples link local planners directly with suppliers and test scenarios together; we should do more of that.

turns.speaker: Harry Metcalfe
turns.text: Practical farming resilience—like reservoirs or water capture—is expensive and needs planning permission and grants; small farms struggle to afford those investments.

chapters.title: Government role: strategy, institutions and policy clarity
chapters.takeaway: Experts say DEFRA lacks clout and continuity; they want a clear food policy, better national coordination and long-term signals to unlock private investment.

turns.speaker: Rupert Lowe
turns.text: Is DEFRA fit for purpose? Farmers need long-term plans, but frequent political change and policy churn create uncertainty for investment.

turns.speaker: Professor Lang
turns.text: We need a proper food policy, not just farming or environment policies. DEFRA is small, politically weak and often lacks the high-level pull to coordinate cross-Government action.

turns.speaker: Professor Ward
turns.text: Resilience is a public good. The state needs to convene industry, farmers and civil society, set long-term targets and fund transformations similar to post-war agricultural efforts.

turns.speaker: Jim Bligh
turns.text: Retailers can form long-term partnerships, but Government must prioritise food as critical infrastructure, consider energy support and be clearer on long-term strategy.

turns.speaker: Professor Lang
turns.text: We suggested renaming DEFRA to reflect food security. We need a national body or committee that can plan cross-departmentally—think Climate Change Committee but for food security.

chapters.title: Practical steps, international lessons and public preparedness
chapters.takeaway: Suggested actions: map and protect key infrastructure, incentivise onshore processing and farming, devolve local powers, educate the public and include communities in planning.

turns.speaker: Matt Turmaine
turns.text: Which countries do this well and what can we learn?

turns.speaker: Professor Ward
turns.text: Look at Finland, Sweden, the Netherlands, Japan and Israel. They take resilience seriously, plan institutionally and link national strategy to local capability.

turns.speaker: Professor Lang
turns.text: Examples vary: Sweden and Finland build public preparedness; France and parts of Belgium have strong regional food partnerships. Multi-level approaches matter.

turns.speaker: Rachel Gilmour
turns.text: How do we protect vulnerable people during disruption and how much is down to households?

turns.speaker: Professor Lang
turns.text: Households help, but community and local partnerships are key. Sweden plans multi-level storage and community support; Britain needs to build similar local capacity and include civil society in planning.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Final point from witnesses?

turns.speaker: Harry Metcalfe
turns.text: My plea is simple: Government should understand farming’s seasonality and long-term nature, and give clearer signals and support so farmers can afford to grow food again.

turns.speaker: Jim Bligh
turns.text: Focus on long-term investment, protect key assets, and recognise food as critical national infrastructure so industry and Government can plan together.

turns.speaker: Professor Ward
turns.text: Treat resilience as a public good, convene a cross-Government effort and match land use to nutritious, resilient production over the next 25 years.

turns.speaker: Professor Lang
turns.text: Strengthen institutions, involve the public, protect supply diversity and unlock financing for resilient infrastructure. Small projects alone won’t be enough.
